name: School dating theory

card.summary: A looksmax.org idea that in school, popularity rather than looks decides who gets dated, so facial attractiveness pays off mainly after school.
card.note: A community theory based on personal observation; no studies of it were found.

quick.overview:
School dating theory is a framework from looksmaxxing forums. It says that in school, girls chase a 'popularity list' and so pick the most popular boys, who are not always the best-looking, while quiet good-looking boys get less attention.

Its payoff for looks is a long-term view: proponents say that after school the ranking switches and good-looking people get an advantage, so appearance work is expected to pay off later, in college and adult dating.
quick.how: It is used as an explanation and a framing, not a routine: forum members cite it to interpret school experiences and to justify focusing on improving looks for later life.
quick.risks: No physical risks. It is an anecdotal theory; no published studies test it.

lead: School dating theory is an idea discussed on looksmax.org that attraction in school follows a popularity hierarchy rather than looks alone. In the original post, the author says popular boys can attract many girls with ease while quieter, better-looking boys receive less attention, because many girls want to be near the top of a popularity list.[1]

The theory helps looks-focused readers by reframing a common frustration: if good looks do not translate into dating success at school, proponents say that reflects status dynamics, and that the advantage of appearance appears after school, in college and adult dating. The post predicts that good-looking men will have a chance with most women there, while the popular but less attractive boy loses his edge.[1] Replies on the thread compare it to celebrity crushes, and one reply attributes it to fame and wealth.[1]

The thread itself rests on personal observation. Adjacent research in developmental psychology separates two kinds of adolescent popularity, likability and status, and studies how each relates to attractiveness and dating.[2][3][4]

chain: Keep improving looks regardless of school results
angle.text: Proponents use the theory to explain why good looks may not translate to dating success at school, and to encourage working on appearance for later life.

infobox: School dating follows popularity; looks matter more after school[1]
Perceived vs sociometric popularity; adolescent attractiveness and dating[2][3][4]

paras: The thread's author describes a 'popularity list' that girls in school are said to chase, and says this explains why a popular boy he regards as less attractive gets many girlfriends while a good-looking, quiet boy gets little attention.[1] He gives his own experience: one girlfriend and a few talking stages, and says the loudest popular girls would not choose him despite his belief that he is better looking and smarter.[1]

The post closes with a prediction: when he goes to college, he expects a shot with most good-looking women in his classes, and expects the popular boy to be without partners after school.[1] The two halves of the theory are therefore a claim about school (status beats looks) and a claim about what follows (looks beat status).

In looks-focused communities the theory works as an explanation and as encouragement. Members use it to interpret school experiences in which attractive peers were passed over, and to justify continuing to improve their appearance for later life. It sits alongside other framework terms in these communities, such as status, frame and 'mogging', that describe how attention is distributed among men.

sections.h: Related research on popularity and attractiveness
paras: Developmental psychologists distinguish sociometric popularity, meaning being well liked, from perceived popularity, meaning social status. The two often diverge: a person can be high in perceived popularity without being broadly liked. Perceived popularity is linked to visibility and dominance, and in some studies to aggression, and psychologist Mitch Prinstein has framed the distinction as likability versus status.[2] A study by Borch, Hyde and Cillessen reported that attractive, overtly aggressive adolescents gained perceived popularity at little cost to being liked, while unattractive aggressors lost on both measures.[2]

A longitudinal study of 78 young adolescents (grades 6 to 8) found that adolescents and their future romantic partners were similar in peer-rated attractiveness before dating began, and that popularity showed the strongest pre-relationship similarity. Adolescents who were low in popularity became more popular after dating a highly popular partner. Adolescents in relationships were rated as more attractive and more popular by peers than non-dating classmates.[3]

A longitudinal study of 1,049 youth rated by observers at grade 3 and grade 9 found that grade 9 looks predicted self-perceived popularity and likability, and progression along a dating and sexual behavior continuum, even after accounting for looks at grade 3.[4] These findings relate appearance to school social standing and dating; none tests the specific claim that popularity outranks looks, or that the pattern reverses after school.
No studies found on school dating theory itself. Related studies of adolescent popularity, attractiveness and dating are described above.[2][3][4]

timeline.event: Longitudinal study reports that adolescent dating partners resemble each other on popularity and attractiveness before dating begins.[3]
Longitudinal study links ninth-grade looks to popularity, likability and dating progression.[4]
The looksmax.org thread 'School dating theory' is posted.[1]

lore.intro: The theory appears in a looksmax.org thread where members trade observations about school popularity and looks.[1]

claims.claim: In school, girls pick by popularity, not looks
claims.believers: The thread author says girls want a shot at the top of a popularity list, which is why popular boys can attract many girls.[1]
claims.experts: Researchers distinguish popularity (status) from likability and report that adolescents in relationships are rated as both more popular and more attractive than non-dating classmates.[2][3] No study has tested whether popularity outranks looks in school dating.

claims.claim: Popular boys do not need to be good-looking
claims.believers: Replies to the thread liken it to celebrity crushes, attributing appeal to fame and wealth.[1]
claims.experts: Research on perceived popularity finds that attractiveness can raise it, particularly alongside dominance or aggression.[2][4]

claims.believers: The author expects to have a shot with most good-looking women at college and later, while the popular boy would lack partners.[1]
claims.experts: Research on adolescence has followed looks into dating progression in ninth grade;[4] no published study has examined this prediction across the transition out of school.

claims.claim: Quiet, good-looking boys get little attention at school
claims.believers: The author reports that he and similar boys receive less attention than popular peers.[1]
claims.experts: A longitudinal study found that ninth-grade looks predicted dating progression after accounting for earlier looks,[4] and another found attractive adolescents were more likely to be dating than classmates who were not.[3]

claims.claim: Dating a popular partner raises your own status
claims.believers: The thread's framing implies girls pursue popular boys for status.[1]
claims.experts: A 2008 study found that low-popularity adolescents became more popular after dating a highly popular partner, while already popular adolescents stayed stable.[3]
